metadata.title: Cost-Normalized Comparison of Password Hashing Algorithms and the Effect of Salting on Rainbow-Table Attacks

MD5.notes: Non-tunable fixed-digest hash. Executes in microseconds without key-stretching.

SHA-256.notes: Non-tunable cryptographic digest designed for raw throughput, not password storage.

PBKDF2.notes: Linear CPU stretching. Calibrated to 800,000 iterations.

bcrypt.notes: Exponential work factor 2^11 (2,048 iterations), 4 KiB memory.

scrypt.notes: Memory-hard function with N=32768 (approx 32.0 MiB RAM).

Argon2id.notes: Argon2id hybrid memory/side-channel resistant with 46.9 MiB RAM, t=4.

MD5.notes: Precomputed table failed completely (0.0% cracked). Salt forced attacker to abandon precomputed lookup.

SHA-256.notes: Precomputed table failed completely (0.0% cracked). Salt forced attacker to abandon precomputed lookup.

phase5_bcrypt_limit.exception_message: password cannot be longer than 72 bytes, truncate manually if necessary (e.g. my_password[:72])
phase5_bcrypt_limit.summary: bcrypt natively considers only the first 72 bytes of input. Passwords differing only after byte 72 collide under standard bcrypt truncation. Modern Python bcrypt libraries throw a ValueError to alert callers. Pre-hashing with SHA-256 fixes the issue by mapping arbitrary-length inputs into 32 bytes.
